designPanel.title: The panel's brief
intro: Before the first design round, an independent panel of three architects proposes the top-level design ([[dec:independent-architects-propose-the-top-level-design]]). You said the context the panel gets is critical, so its brief comes to you before it runs. It follows [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]. The choices that decision leaves open are [[q:P]], [[q:Q]] and [[q:R]]. The panel runs only after you confirm the requirements and approve this brief.

sections.title: Who is on the panel
paragraphs: Three architects. Each is a fresh AI agent on the strongest model available. None has seen the conversations or the planning documents of the agent running the pass, and none sees another's work until the second round. Each has one lens, so that the three proposals differ. A lens says where an architect looks hardest; every architect still answers to every requirement.

items.text: How a live game's facts are held, changed, ordered and recovered across the show machine, the tablets, the phones and the hardware scanners, on a network that drops, with standalone games included.

How designers, venue technicians and outside developers extend the platform without touching the engine's code: games as packs, venues as profiles, new kinds of screen, device and outside program, and the published protocol as what other people build against.

How one owner and AI agents keep the engine easy to understand, change, test and release for years: how small and clear each piece is, and how a change is made, tested on the test bench and shipped with no risk to a show.

sections.title: The blind round
paragraphs: Each architect gets one prepared folder and nothing else:

items.text: As you confirm them on [[page:requirements]]: the ten promises with your answers, the quality targets with the numbers you set, the extension cases and the standing rules.

A show is one game of about two hours at one venue, with a few dozen devices. One show machine, a Raspberry Pi 5, drives the TV and the room's sound and must go from power-on to a running show with no technician. The room's outside programs (video, music, sound with Bluetooth speakers, the venue's lighting) can each crash or be missing. The devices are GM tablets, players' own phones (a web page, with no install and no accounts), hardware scanners and NFC tokens. The venue's Wi-Fi can drop at any moment, and no internet is assumed. A game's content is written in Notion today, with its large media files beside the pack. One owner, who is not an engineer, develops the engine with AI agents, and a future open-source community may join.

items.lead: Your decisions that bind any design
The six decisions ahead, as the agenda
items.text: If you agree ([[q:Q]]). An architect may add, split or merge decisions and must say why. How today's engine moves to the new design waits for the second round, when today's engine is known.

after: Each architect writes a top-level design, decision by decision: the choice; one or two alternatives they rejected, with the cost of each; a table of how the design keeps each promise, meets each quality target and allows each extension case, naming any it cannot meet; its riskiest assumption; and the trial run, a throwaway prototype, that would test that assumption fastest.

sections.title: The second round: meeting today's engine
paragraphs: After the blind round, each architect also gets:

items.text: A fact sheet of what runs where, in what language, and what works today; and the code with its component guides, to read but not change, if you agree ([[q:R]]).

items.lead: The sixteen design flaws, as test situations
items.text: What goes wrong at a show, the problems behind it and where in today's code they sit, with no fix attached.

items.lead: The other two proposals, and the earlier candidate
items.text: The 17-part design drawn bottom-up from today's engine, as one more proposal.

after: Each architect tests every proposal (their own, the other two and the earlier candidate) against the sixteen situations and today's facts: which situations it removes, which it leaves, and what moving today's engine to it would cost. They critique the others, then revise their own design and say what changed and why. The second round also gives the last decision ahead its real options: rebuild beside today's engine, change it in place piece by piece, or a mix.

sections.title: The synthesis
paragraphs: One more agent, who proposed nothing, reads all of it and writes, for each decision ahead: the options the panel found, their costs, where the architects agreed and where they did not, the trial runs worth doing before choosing, and the questions only you can answer. A checker reads the synthesis against the proposals and corrects anything it misstates or leaves out. The synthesis becomes the agenda of the first design round, and a page on this site. The six proposals, three from each round, stay in the repository in full.

sections.title: What is withheld, and how
paragraphs: Withheld from the blind round: the recommendations and leading guesses of the agent running the pass; the earlier candidate, which enters the second round as one more proposal; the earlier lists of design choices; today's engine and its review. Withheld from both rounds: the reasoning of the agent running the pass, the review's conclusions about fixes, and the earlier candidate's table of alternatives.

A script builds each round's folder from the sources (the requirements files, the standing rules, the decision record). Each architect is told to read only its folder, plus the code in the second round, and never the planning documents. Nothing technical stops an agent from opening a file it was told to leave alone, so the synthesis's checker also looks for traces of withheld material in every proposal.

sections.title: Size and cost
paragraphs: About eight agents: three in the blind round, three in the second round, the synthesis and its checker. It takes two to three hours and several million tokens, about the size of one of the larger site workflows.

questions.title: The panel's three lenses
questions.decides: Which lens each of the three independent architects takes, so that their proposals differ where it matters for your goal.
evidence: [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]] fixes three architects with different lenses who propose blind, then critique each other and the earlier candidate. It does not name the lenses.

The draft lenses, on [[page:design#panel|the panel's brief]]: state and authority; growth and extension; living with it. A lens says where an architect looks hardest; every architect still answers to every requirement.

Your goal names three things the design must make easy: maintaining the engine, continuing its development, and extending it. The quality targets add staying up through a live show and standalone and offline play.

options.label: The three draft lenses: state and authority; growth and extension; living with it.
options.cost: Live-show reliability has no architect of its own; it sits inside the state lens.

options.label: Add a fourth architect, on live-show reliability.
options.cost: One more proposal in each round, a longer synthesis, and about a third more time and cost.

options.label: Replace "living with it" with a lens on the smallest possible engine.
options.cost: Keeping the engine easy to maintain and change, which your goal names first, loses its own architect.

questions.recommendation: The three draft lenses. Between them they cover what your goal names, and each quality target still binds all three. A fourth architect adds cost and a longer synthesis for a quality the state lens already weighs.

questions.title: What the panel gets in the blind round
questions.decides: Whether the panel's blind round also gets the decisions you have made that bind any design, and the six decisions ahead as its agenda, or only the goal, the requirements and the setting.
evidence: [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]] lists the goal, the requirements and the setting for the blind round, and names nothing else.

The decisions that bind any design: [[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]], [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]], [[dec:four-words-for-the-game-s-live-facts]], [[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]] and [[dec:the-role-question-starts-from-settled-roles]]. They are your decisions, not the reasoning of the agent running the pass.
The six decisions ahead are your list, from [[dec:design-top-down-hardest-to-reverse-choices-first]].
If anything else should be added to what the panel sees, or kept from it, say so with this question.

options.label: Also give the blind round your binding decisions and the six decisions ahead, with leave to add, split or merge decisions.
options.cost: The agenda frames the architects' thinking; they are told they may change it.

options.label: Give the blind round only the goal, the requirements and the setting.
options.cost: Proposals may break decisions you have already made, and the synthesis must sort them out.

questions.recommendation: Also give the blind round your binding decisions and the six decisions ahead. A panel without them would spend its proposals on designs you have already ruled out, and it may still change the agenda if it says why.

questions.title: The second round reads today's code
questions.decides: Whether, in the second round, the architects may read today's code and its component guides, or only a fact sheet about today's engine.
evidence: [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]] gives the second round today's engine as facts and the sixteen design flaws as test situations. It does not say in what form.
The code is the most exact fact about today's engine. It is also large, and reading it can pull a design toward small changes to today's engine.

options.label: A fact sheet first, then the code and its component guides, to read but not change.
options.cost: The code can pull designs toward today's engine; the architects revise their own blind proposals rather than start again from the code.

options.label: A fact sheet only.
options.cost: The fact sheet is a summary someone wrote; what it leaves out, the architects cannot check.

questions.recommendation: A fact sheet first, then the code, to read only. The architects test their proposals against the real engine, and starting from their own blind proposals keeps the code from setting the design.
